# SC4053 AI Audit Report

**Tokenisation of Real-World and Digital Assets on Ethereum**  
NTU SC4053, AY2026–2027 Semester 1. Evidence cut-off: 6 November 2026 (Asia/Singapore). Baseline revision: `0b1249e`; Phase 6 changes remain uncommitted by explicit instruction.

This report separates executed observations from historical records and remaining acceptance checks. No assignment PDF was found in the repository. The eight section titles below follow the supplied [Phase 6 request](spec/phase6-requirements.md); the team must compare the final submission against the original course brief. The implementation is locally demonstrable, but full submission acceptance remains pending real MetaMask rehearsal and required Sepolia evidence.

## SECTION 1 — Initial Specification & System Scope

The preserved [spec-v0](spec/spec-v0.md) proposes an educational Ethereum application inspired by institutional tokenisation. The motivating problem is fragmented asset registers and manual permission/settlement workflows. The MVP was authorised asset creation, wallet holdings, primary issuance and transfers, on-chain records, and basic issuer compliance. It did not specify every later contract function or frontend screen.

[Spec-v1](spec/spec-v1.md) narrowed the demonstration to fictional property-fund and digital-licensing units. Ethereum provides a shared execution and event layer; ERC-20 fits fungible whole-unit interests, while role-based permissions express issuer/compliance responsibilities. A fixed-price ETH sale avoids pricing oracles and redemption logic and makes delivery/payment atomic within a transaction. None of these choices creates legal title or verifies off-chain custody. There is no institutional integration with the organisations that motivated the proposal.

The actual roles are immutable platform admin, authorised issuer, token default administrator, compliance delegate and investor. The issuer receives a fixed zero-decimal supply. Investors must be eligible to buy or move tokens. The factory creates independent token/sale pairs; sales hold inventory and accounted ETH. React provides marketplace, administration, issuer management and investor portfolio/history.

Later refinements matter: Phase 2 allowed revocation without burning and separated compliance from eligibility; Phase 3 added metadata, registry getters, irreversible sale closure, recovery and forced-ETH handling. D5 added pause and forced transfer while dropping redundant freeze functions. D6 retained issuer admin authority. Phase 5 supplied four-wallet deploy/replay scripts and network configuration. The Phase 6 scenario uses CPT/DLT and two CPT buyers; the preserved Phase 5 replay deliberately remains CPT/DLP with its different quantities.

Excluded: NFTs, yield/dividends, buyback/redemption, NAV oracle, upgradeability, real KYC, verified asset custody, multi-jurisdiction legal compliance and production investment use. A revoked holder can retain a nonzero balance. An administrator can explicitly recover revoked holdings; therefore the historical statement that nobody can alter ownership must be read with this trusted recovery power.

## SECTION 2 — Development Methodology & AI Tooling Infrastructure

The repository uses incremental specifications, typed implementations, tests and evidence files. The [session index](ai-logs/INDEX.md) records Claude research/Claude Code work for foundation, factory/sale, D5 and Phase 5, and Codex work for Phase 2 and Phase 4. These are recorded tool/model labels; this audit does not infer models from chat banners. The index explicitly corrects an earlier Phase 1 model attribution using transcript metadata. Phase 6 was performed in Codex with local shell/file tooling and user-provided IDE context. The exact IDE brand and a full Phase 6 conversation export are not established.

Toolchain inspected and executed: Node 22.18.0/npm 10.9.3 on macOS, Solidity 0.8.24, Hardhat 3.21.0, OpenZeppelin 5.6.1, ethers 6.17.0, React 18.3.1, Vite 6.4.5, Vitest 4.1.12, Mocha/Chai and generated TypeChain types. TypeScript differs by root/frontend (7.0.2/6.0.3). Default and production profiles enable optimizer 200; native Hardhat gas/coverage is used. Slither 0.11.6 and crytic-compile 0.4.2 were installed in an isolated temporary Python environment without replacing Hardhat.

Deployment scripts use Hardhat config variables or encrypted keystore names. Persistent deploys write chain/address/block/code fingerprints and compiled ABIs; local seed fixtures reject public networks. The audit used deterministic local chains and did not read .env secrets or submit public transactions. Git commits/tags preserve phase boundaries; some baseline tags were retrospective, so their names/timestamps alone are not proof of chronology. No nonexistent generic ai-baseline tag is used in this report.

Human decisions are evidenced in D1–D18 and the session index. Chordia Laksh is named in research and decision records; adityamd-1307 is named in merge/implementation records. A commit prefix or merge is not evidence that every line received independent human review. Several reviews were performed by the same model/session that generated code. Phase 6 likewise includes AI self-review and finite tests, not independent professional certification.

**Team completion fields:** [Team: add official student names/IDs and submission responsibilities]; [Team: confirm actual human code-review activities and approvals with evidence]. These are intentionally unfilled rather than invented. Historical workflow deviations—combined test/fix commits and no-commit Codex sessions—remain disclosed in the issue records. Current user instructions prohibit commits, so this phase records raw before/after logs and file hashes instead.

## SECTION 3 — Specification Engineering & Prompt Logs

| Phase | Preserved requirement / prompt evidence | Effect on implementation and evaluation |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Initial architecture | spec-v0, spec-v1 §10, research export and phase1-setup export in ai-logs | Three contracts, fixed price and escrow were human selections among alternatives. Freeze/pause/recovery scope later needed resolution. |
| 2 Token | phase2-requirements.md; curated phase2-session.md | Explicit installed-version review and revocation semantics replaced historical assumptions; `_update` covered delegated movement. |
| 3 Factory/issuance | phase3-requirements.md and c567bbec raw session | D1 renamed APIs; D2 defined metadata; D3 added closure. D6–D8 repaired role liveness, forced ETH and admin policy. |
| 4 Frontend/wallet | phase4-requirements.md; curated phase4-session.md | Built against real compiled ABIs; state invalidation and receipt verification became regression targets. |
| 5 Integration/deployment | phase5-requirements.md; archived 2b56524a session | D11–D18 separated main/replay factories, four wallets and deployment records; network-varying tests exposed AUD-015. |
| 6 Final audit | phase6-requirements.md (verbatim supplied request); ai-logs/phase6-session.md (curated) | Required baseline, threat model, static/manual analysis, adversarial tests, exact demonstration and eight report sections; no fabricated evidence. |

Representative verbatim excerpts from preserved user requirements:

- Phase 2: “Do not implement functionality belonging to later phases.”
- Phase 3: “A successful `createAsset()` should deploy an AssetToken and associated AssetSale, then record the asset in the registry.”
- Phase 4: “Implement all Phase 4 functionality, execute the relevant tests, and update documentation. Do not stop after producing a plan.”
- Phase 5: “Use four distinct MetaMask accounts.”
- Phase 6: “Do not fabricate bugs, prompt logs, screenshots, team contributions, or passing tests.”

The strongest prompt refinement was not adding length but reconciling contradictions: old “every holder is eligible” wording conflicted with later revocation behavior, and immutable issuer addresses did not imply immutable roles. CLAUDE.md accumulates issue-specific rules; AUD-016 now requires both read and signing provider deployment validation. The refined context includes consumers and lifecycle transitions, not only individual functions.

There is no complete verbatim Codex conversation for Phases 2/4 in this repository; curated summaries are labelled as such. Phase 6 preserves the exact request and a work summary, not invented dialogue. [Team: add any separately retained original prompt exports if required by the course.] No claims about hidden model reasoning or unrecorded human contributions are made.

## SECTION 4 — AI-Generated Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Admin[Platform admin] -->|authorize / revoke issuer| F[AssetFactory registry]
  Issuer[Authorised issuer] -->|createAsset| F
  F -->|new: mint to issuer, assign issuer roles| T[AssetToken: ERC20 + AccessControl + Pausable]
  F -->|new: fixed token / issuer / price| S[AssetSale escrow]
  Issuer -->|whitelist sale; approve; allocate| S
  Issuer -->|compliance, pause, recovery| T
  Investor[Eligible investor] -->|exact ETH: buyTokens| S
  S -->|SafeERC20 delivery| T
  S -->|withdraw / sweep ETH| Issuer
  T -->|eligible transfer / transferFrom| Investor
  UI[React dashboards] -->|public reads and logs| RPC[Configured RPC]
  UI -->|checked signing deployment| Wallet[EIP-1193 wallet / BrowserProvider]
  RPC --> F
  RPC --> T
  RPC --> S
  Wallet --> F
  Wallet --> T
  Wallet --> S
```

AssetToken mints only in construction, exposes standard ERC-20/AccessControl APIs, checks both movement endpoints in `_update`, and separates whitelist membership from COMPLIANCE_ROLE. D5 force-transfer requires default admin, nonzero revoked source and eligible destination; it intentionally bypasses pause. Issuer admin cannot be removed. The factory holds no token role.

AssetFactory has no inheritance; its immutable admin authorises issuer addresses. One createAsset transaction deploys two contracts, records sequential ID/metadata/issuer/price, and maps token to sale. Reversion rolls the entire transaction back. It stores plain metadata, not attestations. AssetSale uses SafeERC20, exact quantity-times-price payment and inventory checks; withdrawProceeds clears accounting before issuer.call. sweepExcessETH excludes owed proceeds. Closure is permanent; recovery follows token compliance. No ReentrancyGuard is present or claimed.

WalletContext discovers injected/EIP-6963 providers, invalidates account state on events and fetches roles/balances. Blockchain services read the registry and contracts; writes check fresh conditions and acquire a wallet signer. After SEC-013 both providers validate deployment fingerprints. TransactionContext tracks wallet/submission/receipt outcomes; history decodes bounded genuine event queries and avoids purchase/recovery mislabelling. React renders metadata as text. Public state may be retained while refreshing forms; account state is not reused across wallet sessions.

The architecture is AI-assisted, not attributable entirely to AI: spec-v1 §10 records which proposals were adopted or changed by the team. Checks must live on chain because direct RPC clients bypass every UI restriction. Frontend validation prevents mistakes and improves feedback; it cannot grant security properties absent in contracts.

## SECTION 5 — Problems Discovered & Vulnerability Analysis

The following SEC IDs map one-to-one to existing AUD records. They include security flaws, specification errors and reliability issues. AUD-001–003 were phase-work tracking items, not fabricated vulnerabilities. All historical before/after figures below are cited records, not reruns at old commits in Phase 6.

| ID (legacy) | Component | Severity | Problem | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SEC-001 (AUD-004) | AssetToken | High | Whitelist existed without transfer enforcement | Fixed historically; regression retained | [AUD-004](issues/AUD-004-assettoken-does-not-enforce-transfer-eligibility.md) |
| SEC-002 (AUD-005) | Specification/tests | Medium | Contradictory eligibility invariant and ineffective test | Fixed historically; regression retained | [AUD-005](issues/AUD-005-invariant-1-contradicts-revocation-with-balance-an.md) |
| SEC-003 (AUD-006) | AssetToken / AssetSale | Medium | Issuer admin role loss could strand inventory | Fixed historically; regression retained | [AUD-006](issues/AUD-006-issuer-can-renounce-or-lose-the-admin-role-permane.md) |
| SEC-004 (AUD-007) | AssetSale | Low | Forced ETH had no recovery path | Fixed historically; regression retained | [AUD-007](issues/AUD-007-eth-forced-into-assetsale-is-unrecoverable.md) |
| SEC-005 (AUD-008) | Factory policy | Low | Platform admin could authorise itself as issuer | Fixed historically; regression retained | [AUD-008](issues/AUD-008-platform-admin-can-authorise-itself-as-an-issuer.md) |
| SEC-006 (AUD-009) | Frontend state | Low | Approval refresh erased the deposit quantity | Fixed historically; regression retained | [AUD-009](issues/AUD-009-issuer-inventory-form-loses-quantity-after-allowan.md) |
| SEC-007 (AUD-010) | Frontend transactions | Medium | Receipt timeout was displayed as transaction failure | Fixed historically; regression retained | [AUD-010](issues/AUD-010-receipt-timeout-incorrectly-reported-as-transactio.md) |
| SEC-008 (AUD-011) | Build reproducibility | Medium | Frontend lockfile omitted platform packages | Fixed historically; regression retained | [AUD-011](issues/AUD-011-frontend-lockfile-omits-non-macos-platform-binarie.md) |
| SEC-009 (AUD-012) | Deployment configuration | Low | Sepolia script omitted optimized build profile | Fixed historically; regression retained | [AUD-012](issues/AUD-012-assetfactory-is-exactly-at-the-eip-170-size-limit-.md) |
| SEC-010 (AUD-013) | Frontend history | Low | Forced transfer was mislabeled as holder transfer | Fixed historically; regression retained | [AUD-013](issues/AUD-013-transaction-history-shows-a-forced-transfer-as-an-.md) |
| SEC-011 (AUD-014) | Build configuration | Low | Default build retained the factory size risk | Fixed historically; regression retained | [AUD-014](issues/AUD-014-default-build-profile-leaves-assetfactory-at-the-e.md) |
| SEC-012 (AUD-015) | Frontend test isolation | Low | Unit tests depended on generated deployment network | Fixed historically; regression retained | [AUD-015](issues/AUD-015-frontend-unit-tests-fail-once-the-committed-deploy.md) |
| SEC-013 (AUD-016) | Frontend signer | Medium | Signing RPC deployment was not verified | Fixed in Phase 6 working tree | [AUD-016](issues/AUD-016-signing-wallet-deployment-is-not-checked-against-t.md) |

### SEC-001 — Whitelist existed without transfer enforcement (High; AUD-004)

**1. Why AI made the mistake**

The preserved Phase 1 source explicitly called itself a placeholder. Later transfer behavior demonstrated the gap; it should not be portrayed as a failed attempt to implement completed compliance.

**2. Why it is problematic**

Inherited transfer accepted unapproved recipients. A mapping and skipped tests did not protect on-chain movement.

**3. How the issue was fixed**

Phase 2 added AccessControl and endpoint checks in the OpenZeppelin _update hook, including delegated transfers, while minting only to the designated issuer.

**4. Evidence that the fix works**

AssetToken.regression.test.ts; phase2/before.log: 0 passing/1 failing, regression-after.log: 1 passing. Current 153-test run retains the regression. See the [full finding and evidence links](issues/AUD-004-assettoken-does-not-enforce-transfer-eligibility.md).

### SEC-002 — Contradictory eligibility invariant and ineffective test (Medium; AUD-005)

**1. Why AI made the mistake**

The Phase 3 prompt repeated the old invariant while later Phase 2 requirements permitted revocation with a balance. The issue record documents that the implementation did not reconcile these statements.

**2. Why it is problematic**

A passing test purported to establish that every holder was approved, although revocation made that property false by design.

**3. How the issue was fixed**

Restated eligibility as a movement restriction, preserved the revoked balance, and exercised revoke/send/receive/buy/reapprove behavior.

**4. Evidence that the fix works**

Phase3.regression.test.ts AUD-005; recorded before: 99 passing/1 failing; after at 0f9ce3f: 100 passing. See the [full finding and evidence links](issues/AUD-005-invariant-1-contradicts-revocation-with-balance-an.md).

### SEC-003 — Issuer admin role loss could strand inventory (Medium; AUD-006)

**1. Why AI made the mistake**

Phase 2 documented role loss; the Phase 3 recovery reasoning assumed deployment-time roles remained. Hypothesis: mutable role state was omitted from lifecycle reasoning.

**2. Why it is problematic**

Losing all administrators after revoking issuer or sale eligibility could leave nobody able to restore eligibility for recovery.

**3. How the issue was fixed**

D6 prevents removal or renunciation of the immutable issuer’s default admin role. Compliance remains delegable/revocable, and the issuer can restore it.

**4. Evidence that the fix works**

Phase3.regression.test.ts AUD-006 role paths; historical before 100 passing/3 failing, after 103 passing. Current revoked-endpoint recovery test also passes. See the [full finding and evidence links](issues/AUD-006-issuer-can-renounce-or-lose-the-admin-role-permane.md).

### SEC-004 — Forced ETH had no recovery path (Low; AUD-007)

**1. Why AI made the mistake**

The Phase 3 report equated absence of receive/fallback with inability to receive ETH. The transcript-backed issue identifies this false assumption.

**2. Why it is problematic**

Forced ETH was stranded; accounted buyer proceeds were not lost. An equality-based ETH invariant was also inaccurate.

**3. How the issue was fixed**

D7 added issuer-only sweepExcessETH for balance minus owed proceeds and corrected the invariant.

**4. Evidence that the fix works**

Phase3.regression.test.ts AUD-007: historical 3 failures then 107 total passes. Phase 6 adds three passing cross-function/rejecting callback tests. See the [full finding and evidence links](issues/AUD-007-eth-forced-into-assetsale-is-unrecoverable.md).

### SEC-005 — Platform admin could authorise itself as issuer (Low; AUD-008)

**1. Why AI made the mistake**

The function table omitted the restriction stated in the roles table. The issue record shows implementation followed the former without a cross-check.

**2. Why it is problematic**

One address could combine platform and issuer powers against the stated policy. This was never Sybil-resistant separation.

**3. How the issue was fixed**

D8 rejects authorizeIssuer(admin). Documentation acknowledges second-wallet and investor-whitelisting limitations.

**4. Evidence that the fix works**

Phase3.regression.test.ts AUD-008; historical before 107 passing/1 failing; after 108 passing. See the [full finding and evidence links](issues/AUD-008-platform-admin-can-authorise-itself-as-an-issuer.md).

### SEC-006 — Approval refresh erased the deposit quantity (Low; AUD-009)

**1. Why AI made the mistake**

The generated client cleared public registry data and account data using the same lifecycle, unmounting issuer management after confirmation.

**2. Why it is problematic**

The required two-transaction inventory flow lost its form input between approval and deposit. Tokens and permissions were not compromised.

**3. How the issue was fixed**

Keep the public registry during refresh so the manager stays mounted; still invalidate private account state and preflight writes.

**4. Evidence that the fix works**

issuer.test.tsx separate approval/deposit test; phase4/frontend-tests-third.log: 102 passing/1 failing; after-refresh-fix.log: 103 passing. See the [full finding and evidence links](issues/AUD-009-issuer-inventory-form-loses-quantity-after-allowan.md).

### SEC-007 — Receipt timeout was displayed as transaction failure (Medium; AUD-010)

**1. Why AI made the mistake**

The generated transaction handler distinguished rejection but grouped unavailable receipts with failures. The regression isolated TIMEOUT after submission.

**2. Why it is problematic**

A transaction could still mine after the user saw failure and retried, leading to unintended repeated purchases.

**3. How the issue was fixed**

Keep the submitted hash, show unconfirmed status, disable repeats within the session and explicitly recheck the receipt.

**4. Evidence that the fix works**

ui.test.tsx timed-out transaction test; phase4/receipt-timeout-before.log fails; subsequent frontend logs pass. Current full suite 122 passing. See the [full finding and evidence links](issues/AUD-010-receipt-timeout-incorrectly-reported-as-transactio.md).

### SEC-008 — Frontend lockfile omitted platform packages (Medium; AUD-011)

**1. Why AI made the mistake**

The recorded clean install was on macOS only. The issue labels npm rewriting an existing dependency tree as a hypothesis, not a proven hidden cause.

**2. Why it is problematic**

Windows npm ci failed due to missing optional package entries; a single-machine install did not establish portability.

**3. How the issue was fixed**

Regenerated lock metadata without changing resolved versions; regression checks all optional dependencies have entries.

**4. Evidence that the fix works**

FrontendLockfile.regression.test.ts; aud-011/npm-ci-before.log and npm-ci-after.log document an actual Windows fail/pass. Current regression passes; no new cross-OS install claim. See the [full finding and evidence links](issues/AUD-011-frontend-lockfile-omits-non-macos-platform-binarie.md).

### SEC-009 — Sepolia script omitted optimized build profile (Low; AUD-012)

**1. Why AI made the mistake**

Phase 1 configured a production profile but the deploy script did not select it. Later contract growth reached the size limit without a profile check.

**2. Why it is problematic**

Factory runtime was exactly 24,576 bytes, leaving no growth headroom. It still deployed at equality; the issue was not an observed oversized rejection at that revision.

**3. How the issue was fixed**

Explicitly selected the optimized production profile for Sepolia deployment.

**4. Evidence that the fix works**

DeployProfile.regression.test.ts; aud-012 deploy logs: 24,576 to 13,545 runtime bytes. Historical 1 regression failure then 129 total passes. See the [full finding and evidence links](issues/AUD-012-assetfactory-is-exactly-at-the-eip-170-size-limit-.md).

### SEC-010 — Forced transfer was mislabeled as holder transfer (Low; AUD-013)

**1. Why AI made the mistake**

The old history consumer was correct before D5. Adding forced-transfer semantics changed the meaning of Transfer events; existing mocks did not include the new event.

**2. Why it is problematic**

The UI attributed an administrator recovery/confiscation to the holder’s ordinary transfer activity.

**3. How the issue was fixed**

Query and label ForcedTransfer and remove its companion Transfer row by transaction/from/to/amount.

**4. Evidence that the fix works**

history.test.ts before 1 failing/4 passing; aud-013/frontend-tests-after.log: 113 passing; real-chain lifecycle verifies typed deduplication. See the [full finding and evidence links](issues/AUD-013-transaction-history-shows-a-forced-transfer-as-an-.md).

### SEC-011 — Default build retained the factory size risk (Low; AUD-014)

**1. Why AI made the mistake**

AUD-012 intentionally addressed the requested Sepolia path only. The remaining default-profile risk was recorded, then separately addressed; it was not concealed.

**2. Why it is problematic**

Local deployment, tests, demos and frontend artifact consumers remained at the EIP-170 boundary until all build paths were fixed.

**3. How the issue was fixed**

Enabled optimizer runs=200 in the default profile and guarded all compiling npm-script paths.

**4. Evidence that the fix works**

DeployProfile.regression.test.ts; AUD-014 before 131 passing/1 failing, after 132 passing. Fresh Phase 6 default and production builds both measure factory 13,545 bytes. See the [full finding and evidence links](issues/AUD-014-default-build-profile-leaves-assetfactory-at-the-e.md).

### SEC-012 — Unit tests depended on generated deployment network (Low; AUD-015)

**1. Why AI made the mistake**

The mock wallet assumed chain 31337 while production configuration read the latest deployment file. Phase 5 made that file change networks.

**2. Why it is problematic**

A genuine Sepolia configuration would break otherwise-correct local tests and invalidate reproducibility claims.

**3. How the issue was fixed**

Mock fixed test deployment data in unit setup, retain real ABIs, and keep integration on its own actual deployment.

**4. Evidence that the fix works**

deploymentIsolation.regression.test.ts; aud-015 reports 40 failing with the new test/Sepolia config before, 118 passing after. Current 122 frontend passes. See the [full finding and evidence links](issues/AUD-015-frontend-unit-tests-fail-once-the-committed-deploy.md).

### SEC-013 — Signing RPC deployment was not verified (Medium; AUD-016)

**1. Why AI made the mistake**

The Phase 4 code validated deployment only on its public read provider. Exact author reasoning is not preserved. Hypothesis: matching chain IDs were treated as matching deployment identity.

**2. Why it is problematic**

Two local nodes can share chain ID and deterministic addresses; users could sign against a different or absent contract from the one displayed.

**3. How the issue was fixed**

Apply code/block fingerprint validation to the BrowserProvider and recheck its account and chain before returning the signer.

**4. Evidence that the fix works**

signingDeployment.security.test.ts: 4 failures before, 4 passing after within the 122-test suite. Real-chain frontend integration passes with the new signer checks. See the [full finding and evidence links](issues/AUD-016-signing-wallet-deployment-is-not-checked-against-t.md).

Scanner findings are reported separately: 29 results, individually triaged, with no confirmed new production-contract exploit. `allocate`'s high arbitrary-source warning is a false positive because the source is immutable issuer and the caller/allowance are restricted. The other high warning is an intentionally minimal test holder. Exact zero checks are valid; callback-event ordering does not establish double payout. Development dependency warnings, issuer trust, unsupported directly deployed tokens, scalability and potential compiler applicability are disclosed in [security findings](audit/security-findings.md), [Slither summary](audit/slither-summary.md) and [dependency review](audit/dependency-review.md). They are not counted as fixed exploits.

## SECTION 6 — Validation Process & Testing Strategy

[Baseline](audit/baseline-results.md): 142 contract/script and 118 frontend tests, successful builds and existing demos. The first compile was blocked by a sandbox cache lock, then rerun with cache access. The initial state was recorded before production changes.

Final executed commands: `npm test` — 153 pass; `npm test --prefix frontend` — 122 pass; `npm run test:integration` — one real-chain service lifecycle pass; `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npm run build --prefix frontend` — pass. The targeted new security suite has 11 passing tests. The four new frontend regression cases initially failed, then passed after SEC-013. Local deployment, seed scripts, default and production compilation passed. Full command exits/raw logs are in [test-results.md](audit/test-results.md).

Unit tests validate individual guards, errors, events and state. Integration deploys real local contracts and drives production frontend services via an EIP-1193 adapter. Access-control matrices exercise outsiders/platform admin across separate issuers. Callback harnesses attempt recursive and cross-function ETH withdrawals and rejection. Payment boundaries include checked uint256 overflow and no-ETH RPC admission. Three seeds each execute 48 operations over two assets, tracking balances, inventory, proceeds, failures and revocation. This controlled model detects conservation/isolation regressions but is not exhaustive fuzzing or proof.

Native `npx hardhat test --coverage` reports 100% lines and statements for each production contract; including helpers, 99.25% lines/99.37% statements. No branch-completeness or frontend coverage claim is made. `--gas-stats` provides measured fixture ranges. Slither scanned 22 contracts with 102 detectors and produced genuine machine output (`success:true`, exit 255 due to findings). Dependency audits and a value-redacting tracked-file secret scan complement source review. Slither's [official project](https://github.com/crytic/slither) describes its supported workflow; this audit verified the installed tool against the actual build artifacts.

The exact local Phase 6 demo passed 31 checks across 18 mined transactions, including three expected reverts. It confirms issuer/A/B/sale CPT balances 9850/80/70/0, fixed supply 10000, 0.15 ETH withdrawn and DLT isolation. Hashes, event logs and fee-adjusted failure state are in [final-demo.json](audit/final-demo.json).

Two new audit-harness errors were caught: a TypeChain overload mismatch and assumption that revert names were always decoded. Both first failures and corrected reruns remain in evidence. This demonstrates why generated validation code also needs validation. No browser was connected; no screenshots, actual MetaMask transaction, or Sepolia deployment was executed. Existing AUD-002/003 remain open acceptance work. Tests cannot establish off-chain asset truth, all call sequences, dishonest-provider safety or absence of compiler defects.

## SECTION 7 — Improvements & Refinements

Historical refinements include transfer-hook enforcement, role-recovery liveness, separate forced-ETH accounting, form persistence, unknown-receipt handling, portable lock metadata, event attribution and network-independent fixtures. D5 introduced explicit recovery powers after user decision, not as an undocumented audit “fix”. The historical optimized factory reduction is 24,576 to 13,545 bytes; older unoptimized gas measurements should not be compared indiscriminately with current runs.

Phase 6 changed only two production frontend files: Blockchain validates the signing provider as well as the read provider and rechecks account/network; AppLayout names the configured network instead of hardcoding a previous development phase. Production Solidity and dependency versions are unchanged. New tests, local demo, static triage, threat model and reports make the result reviewable. Source/ABI inventory and file hashes provide reproducibility without prohibited commits.

Current runtime sizes are factory 13,545, token 4,124 and sale 3,132 bytes. Current gas observations include factory deployment 2,973,114, createAsset 1,925,522–2,013,385 and buyTokens 55,057–89,269. No new gas optimization or savings is claimed; removing storage or compliance checks without a measured justified benefit would change behavior. Additional wallet RPC reads are a deliberate correctness cost. No unrelated product features were added.

## SECTION 8 — Lessons Learned

AI was useful for translating staged requirements into typed contracts/services, generating test fixtures, producing repeatable scripts and drafting documentation linked to evidence. The history supports breadth and iteration, not a measured productivity multiplier. There are no recorded human-only time estimates, so acceleration is qualitative.

Generated code and generated tests can share the same wrong assumption. A whitelist mapping without a hook compiled, a test with an invariant in its name missed revocation, and event consumers passed after contract semantics changed. Likewise, deployment identity checked on one RPC did not establish identity on the signing RPC. Tests should cross boundaries and challenge assumptions rather than mirror implementation branches.

Complete specifications must define revocation, delegation, recovery, callback behavior, transaction uncertainty and configuration changes. Contradictions need explicit precedence and recorded decisions. The team's preserved D decisions and issue-specific rules are more useful than treating an initial prompt as immutable truth. Recovery powers also reveal a real trade-off: compliance and liveness require trusted administrators, so the application should never claim issuer-free ownership guarantees.

Independent tools add evidence but require interpretation. Slither flagged legitimate immutable-source transfer logic and deliberate test helpers; dismissing all warnings or calling their count proof of insecurity would both be wrong. Coverage shows execution, not sufficient assertions. Dependency severity must be assessed by runtime reachability, while remaining compiler advisories must be acknowledged even when no exploit is reproduced.

If starting again, the team should define lifecycle invariants before generation, preserve original prompts automatically with safe redaction, separate implementation from independent review, test every deployment profile and provider boundary, and schedule real MetaMask/testnet acceptance before the final reporting phase. Regression tests should fail for behavioral reasons on the original implementation; historical failures and workflow deviations should remain visible. Human owners must approve privileged recovery semantics, protect keys, verify real assets if ever applicable, and sign off the final demonstration. AI output is a draft that earns confidence through review and evidence, not an authority that transfers responsibility away from the developers.

8	## SECTION 1 — Initial Specification & System Scope

10	The preserved [spec-v0](spec/spec-v0.md) proposes an educational Ethereum application inspired by institutional tokenisation. The motivating problem is fragmented asset registers and manual permission/settlement workflows. The MVP was authorised asset creation, wallet holdings, primary issuance and transfers, on-chain records, and basic issuer compliance. It did not specify every later contract function or frontend screen.
11	
12	[Spec-v1](spec/spec-v1.md) narrowed the demonstration to fictional property-fund and digital-licensing units. Ethereum provides a shared execution and event layer; ERC-20 fits fungible whole-unit interests, while role-based permissions express issuer/compliance responsibilities. A fixed-price ETH sale avoids pricing oracles and redemption logic and makes delivery/payment atomic within a transaction. None of these choices creates legal title or verifies off-chain custody. There is no institutional integration with the organisations that motivated the proposal.
13	
14	The actual roles are immutable platform admin, authorised issuer, token default administrator, compliance delegate and investor. The issuer receives a fixed zero-decimal supply. Investors must be eligible to buy or move tokens. The factory creates independent token/sale pairs; sales hold inventory and accounted ETH. React provides marketplace, administration, issuer management and investor portfolio/history.
15	
16	Later refinements matter: Phase 2 allowed revocation without burning and separated compliance from eligibility; Phase 3 added metadata, registry getters, irreversible sale closure, recovery and forced-ETH handling. D5 added pause and forced transfer while dropping redundant freeze functions. D6 retained issuer admin authority. Phase 5 supplied four-wallet deploy/replay scripts and network configuration. The Phase 6 scenario uses CPT/DLT and two CPT buyers; the preserved Phase 5 replay deliberately remains CPT/DLP with its different quantities.
17	
18	Excluded: NFTs, yield/dividends, buyback/redemption, NAV oracle, upgradeability, real KYC, verified asset custody, multi-jurisdiction legal compliance and production investment use. A revoked holder can retain a nonzero balance. An administrator can explicitly recover revoked holdings; therefore the historical statement that nobody can alter ownership must be read with this trusted recovery power.

259	Factory runtime was exactly 24,576 bytes, leaving no growth headroom. It still deployed at equality; the issue was not an observed oversized rejection at that revision.
260	
261	**3. How the issue was fixed**
262	
263	Explicitly selected the optimized production profile for Sepolia deployment.
264	
265	**4. Evidence that the fix works**
266	
267	DeployProfile.regression.test.ts; aud-012 deploy logs: 24,576 to 13,545 runtime bytes. Historical 1 regression failure then 129 total passes. See the [full finding and evidence links](issues/AUD-012-assetfactory-is-exactly-at-the-eip-170-size-limit-.md).
268	
269	### SEC-010 — Forced transfer was mislabeled as holder transfer (Low; AUD-013)
270	
271	**1. Why AI made the mistake**
272	
273	The old history consumer was correct before D5. Adding forced-transfer semantics changed the meaning of Transfer events; existing mocks did not include the new event.
274	
275	**2. Why it is problematic**
276	
277	The UI attributed an administrator recovery/confiscation to the holder’s ordinary transfer activity.
278	
279	**3. How the issue was fixed**
280	
281	Query and label ForcedTransfer and remove its companion Transfer row by transaction/from/to/amount.
282	
283	**4. Evidence that the fix works**
284	
285	history.test.ts before 1 failing/4 passing; aud-013/frontend-tests-after.log: 113 passing; real-chain lifecycle verifies typed deduplication. See the [full finding and evidence links](issues/AUD-013-transaction-history-shows-a-forced-transfer-as-an-.md).
286	
287	### SEC-011 — Default build retained the factory size risk (Low; AUD-014)
288	
289	**1. Why AI made the mistake**
290	
291	AUD-012 intentionally addressed the requested Sepolia path only. The remaining default-profile risk was recorded, then separately addressed; it was not concealed.
292	
293	**2. Why it is problematic**
294	
295	Local deployment, tests, demos and frontend artifact consumers remained at the EIP-170 boundary until all build paths were fixed.
296	
297	**3. How the issue was fixed**
298	
299	Enabled optimizer runs=200 in the default profile and guarded all compiling npm-script paths.
300	
301	**4. Evidence that the fix works**
302	
303	DeployProfile.regression.test.ts; AUD-014 before 131 passing/1 failing, after 132 passing. Fresh Phase 6 default and production builds both measure factory 13,545 bytes. See the [full finding and evidence links](issues/AUD-014-default-build-profile-leaves-assetfactory-at-the-e.md).
304	
305	### SEC-012 — Unit tests depended on generated deployment network (Low; AUD-015)
306	
307	**1. Why AI made the mistake**
308	
309	The mock wallet assumed chain 31337 while production configuration read the latest deployment file. Phase 5 made that file change networks.
310	
311	**2. Why it is problematic**
312	
313	A genuine Sepolia configuration would break otherwise-correct local tests and invalidate reproducibility claims.
314	
315	**3. How the issue was fixed**
316	
317	Mock fixed test deployment data in unit setup, retain real ABIs, and keep integration on its own actual deployment.
318	
319	**4. Evidence that the fix works**
320	
321	deploymentIsolation.regression.test.ts; aud-015 reports 40 failing with the new test/Sepolia config before, 118 passing after. Current 122 frontend passes. See the [full finding and evidence links](issues/AUD-015-frontend-unit-tests-fail-once-the-committed-deploy.md).

323	### SEC-013 — Signing RPC deployment was not verified (Medium; AUD-016)
324	
325	**1. Why AI made the mistake**
326	
327	The Phase 4 code validated deployment only on its public read provider. Exact author reasoning is not preserved. Hypothesis: matching chain IDs were treated as matching deployment identity.
328	
329	**2. Why it is problematic**
330	
331	Two local nodes can share chain ID and deterministic addresses; users could sign against a different or absent contract from the one displayed.
332	
333	**3. How the issue was fixed**
334	
335	Apply code/block fingerprint validation to the BrowserProvider and recheck its account and chain before returning the signer.
336	
337	**4. Evidence that the fix works**
338	
339	signingDeployment.security.test.ts: 4 failures before, 4 passing after within the 122-test suite. Real-chain frontend integration passes with the new signer checks. See the [full finding and evidence links](issues/AUD-016-signing-wallet-deployment-is-not-checked-against-t.md).
340	
341	Scanner findings are reported separately: 29 results, individually triaged, with no confirmed new production-contract exploit. `allocate`'s high arbitrary-source warning is a false positive because the source is immutable issuer and the caller/allowance are restricted. The other high warning is an intentionally minimal test holder. Exact zero checks are valid; callback-event ordering does not establish double payout. Development dependency warnings, issuer trust, unsupported directly deployed tokens, scalability and potential compiler applicability are disclosed in [security findings](audit/security-findings.md), [Slither summary](audit/slither-summary.md) and [dependency review](audit/dependency-review.md). They are not counted as fixed exploits.
342	
343	## SECTION 6 — Validation Process & Testing Strategy
344	
345	[Baseline](audit/baseline-results.md): 142 contract/script and 118 frontend tests, successful builds and existing demos. The first compile was blocked by a sandbox cache lock, then rerun with cache access. The initial state was recorded before production changes.
346	
347	Final executed commands: `npm test` — 153 pass; `npm test --prefix frontend` — 122 pass; `npm run test:integration` — one real-chain service lifecycle pass; `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npm run build --prefix frontend` — pass. The targeted new security suite has 11 passing tests. The four new frontend regression cases initially failed, then passed after SEC-013. Local deployment, seed scripts, default and production compilation passed. Full command exits/raw logs are in [test-results.md](audit/test-results.md).
348	
349	Unit tests validate individual guards, errors, events and state. Integration deploys real local contracts and drives production frontend services via an EIP-1193 adapter. Access-control matrices exercise outsiders/platform admin across separate issuers. Callback harnesses attempt recursive and cross-function ETH withdrawals and rejection. Payment boundaries include checked uint256 overflow and no-ETH RPC admission. Three seeds each execute 48 operations over two assets, tracking balances, inventory, proceeds, failures and revocation. This controlled model detects conservation/isolation regressions but is not exhaustive fuzzing or proof.
350	
351	Native `npx hardhat test --coverage` reports 100% lines and statements for each production contract; including helpers, 99.25% lines/99.37% statements. No branch-completeness or frontend coverage claim is made. `--gas-stats` provides measured fixture ranges. Slither scanned 22 contracts with 102 detectors and produced genuine machine output (`success:true`, exit 255 due to findings). Dependency audits and a value-redacting tracked-file secret scan complement source review. Slither's [official project](https://github.com/crytic/slither) describes its supported workflow; this audit verified the installed tool against the actual build artifacts.
352	
353	The exact local Phase 6 demo passed 31 checks across 18 mined transactions, including three expected reverts. It confirms issuer/A/B/sale CPT balances 9850/80/70/0, fixed supply 10000, 0.15 ETH withdrawn and DLT isolation. Hashes, event logs and fee-adjusted failure state are in [final-demo.json](audit/final-demo.json).
354	
355	Two new audit-harness errors were caught: a TypeChain overload mismatch and assumption that revert names were always decoded. Both first failures and corrected reruns remain in evidence. This demonstrates why generated validation code also needs validation. No browser was connected; no screenshots, actual MetaMask transaction, or Sepolia deployment was executed. Existing AUD-002/003 remain open acceptance work. Tests cannot establish off-chain asset truth, all call sequences, dishonest-provider safety or absence of compiler defects.
356	
357	## SECTION 7 — Improvements & Refinements
358	
359	Historical refinements include transfer-hook enforcement, role-recovery liveness, separate forced-ETH accounting, form persistence, unknown-receipt handling, portable lock metadata, event attribution and network-independent fixtures. D5 introduced explicit recovery powers after user decision, not as an undocumented audit “fix”. The historical optimized factory reduction is 24,576 to 13,545 bytes; older unoptimized gas measurements should not be compared indiscriminately with current runs.
360	
361	Phase 6 changed only two production frontend files: Blockchain validates the signing provider as well as the read provider and rechecks account/network; AppLayout names the configured network instead of hardcoding a previous development phase. Production Solidity and dependency versions are unchanged. New tests, local demo, static triage, threat model and reports make the result reviewable. Source/ABI inventory and file hashes provide reproducibility without prohibited commits.
362	
363	Current runtime sizes are factory 13,545, token 4,124 and sale 3,132 bytes. Current gas observations include factory deployment 2,973,114, createAsset 1,925,522–2,013,385 and buyTokens 55,057–89,269. No new gas optimization or savings is claimed; removing storage or compliance checks without a measured justified benefit would change behavior. Additional wallet RPC reads are a deliberate correctness cost. No unrelated product features were added.
364	
365	## SECTION 8 — Lessons Learned
366	
367	AI was useful for translating staged requirements into typed contracts/services, generating test fixtures, producing repeatable scripts and drafting documentation linked to evidence. The history supports breadth and iteration, not a measured productivity multiplier. There are no recorded human-only time estimates, so acceleration is qualitative.
368	
369	Generated code and generated tests can share the same wrong assumption. A whitelist mapping without a hook compiled, a test with an invariant in its name missed revocation, and event consumers passed after contract semantics changed. Likewise, deployment identity checked on one RPC did not establish identity on the signing RPC. Tests should cross boundaries and challenge assumptions rather than mirror implementation branches.
370	
371	Complete specifications must define revocation, delegation, recovery, callback behavior, transaction uncertainty and configuration changes. Contradictions need explicit precedence and recorded decisions. The team's preserved D decisions and issue-specific rules are more useful than treating an initial prompt as immutable truth. Recovery powers also reveal a real trade-off: compliance and liveness require trusted administrators, so the application should never claim issuer-free ownership guarantees.
372	
373	Independent tools add evidence but require interpretation. Slither flagged legitimate immutable-source transfer logic and deliberate test helpers; dismissing all warnings or calling their count proof of insecurity would both be wrong. Coverage shows execution, not sufficient assertions. Dependency severity must be assessed by runtime reachability, while remaining compiler advisories must be acknowledged even when no exploit is reproduced.
374	
375	If starting again, the team should define lifecycle invariants before generation, preserve original prompts automatically with safe redaction, separate implementation from independent review, test every deployment profile and provider boundary, and schedule real MetaMask/testnet acceptance before the final reporting phase. Regression tests should fail for behavioral reasons on the original implementation; historical failures and workflow deviations should remain visible. Human owners must approve privileged recovery semantics, protect keys, verify real assets if ever applicable, and sign off the final demonstration. AI output is a draft that earns confidence through review and evidence, not an authority that transfers responsibility away from the developers.

The assignment PDF was absent; the team must check course packaging and complete identity/contribution fields in the AI report.

Production use would require independent review, resolution of compiler/dependency concerns, key governance/recovery design, verified legal/custody arrangements and stronger operational monitoring. Registry/history pagination, durable pending-transaction tracking and explicit UI pause status are possible future refinements. They are not implemented features. The present system is an academic local demonstration, not a production investment platform.

1	# Final Technical Report
2	
3	Tokenisation of Real-World and Digital Assets on Ethereum — NTU SC4053, AY2026–2027 Semester 1. Reviewed 6 November 2026 (Asia/Singapore), starting revision `0b1249e`. Phase 6 changes are uncommitted by instruction.
4	
5	## Problem and scope
6	
7	The project demonstrates programmable issuance, settlement and transfer permissions for fictional property and digital-licensing units. Fragmented ownership records and manual eligibility checks motivate a shared on-chain register. The system records ERC-20 balances and transaction events; it does not verify custody, perform real KYC, or establish enforceable legal ownership. Prices and assets are simulated. No institutional integrations, redemption, yield, price oracle, NFTs or upgradeable contracts are implemented.
8	
9	The initial proposal is preserved in [spec-v0](spec/spec-v0.md). [Spec-v1](spec/spec-v1.md), later phase requirements and decisions D1–D18 specify the implemented behavior. Later explicit requirements supersede historical API names and revocation rules.
10	
11	## Architecture
12	
13	```mermaid
14	flowchart LR
15	  A[Platform administrator] -->|issuer authorisation| F[AssetFactory]
16	  I[Authorised issuer] -->|createAsset| F
17	  F -->|deploy and register| T[AssetToken]
18	  F -->|deploy and register| S[AssetSale]
19	  I -->|whitelist and approve| T
20	  I -->|allocate inventory| S
21	  B[Approved investor] -->|exact ETH payment| S
22	  S -->|deliver tokens| T
23	  T -->|eligible transfers| B
24	  S -->|withdraw proceeds / recover inventory| I
25	  UI[React dashboards] -->|reads and events| RPC[Configured public RPC]
26	  UI -->|sign transactions| W[EIP-1193 wallet]
27	  RPC --> F
28	  RPC --> T
29	  RPC --> S
30	  W --> F
31	  W --> T
32	  W --> S
33	```
34	
35	The factory creates an independent token and sale for each asset in one transaction. Neither the factory nor platform admin receives token administration by deployment. Token and sale issuer addresses refer to the authorised creator. No proxies or shared asset balances exist.
36	
37	## Contract design and interface
38	
39	| Contract | State / inheritance | Public operations and restrictions |
40	|---|---|---|
41	| AssetFactory | Immutable admin, authorisedIssuers, tokenToSale, private asset array; no inheritance | Admin calls authorizeIssuer/revokeIssuer. Authorised issuer calls createAsset. Anyone reads getAsset/getAssetCount and public getters. |
42	| AssetToken | ERC20, AccessControl, Pausable; immutable issuer, whitelist mapping, COMPLIANCE_ROLE | ERC-20 transfer/transferFrom/approve and getters; setWhitelisted requires compliance role; pause/unpause/forcedTransfer require default admin; inherited grantRole/revokeRole/renounceRole govern delegation. |
43	| AssetSale | SafeERC20 library; immutable assetToken, issuer and pricePerToken; unclaimedProceeds, saleClosed | Issuer calls allocate, withdrawProceeds, sweepExcessETH, closeSale, recoverUnsoldTokens. Eligible buyers call payable buyTokens. Anyone reads availableTokens and public getters. |
44	
45	The full ABI-derived function inventory, including inherited functions and mutability, is [contract-inventory.json](audit/contract-inventory.json).
46	
47	AssetToken has zero decimals and mints a positive fixed supply only in its constructor. The designated issuer is initially whitelisted and receives default admin and compliance roles. `_update` enforces sender and recipient eligibility and pause state for direct/delegated movements, including zero-value transfers. Spender eligibility is intentionally irrelevant: allowance and holder/recipient eligibility are required. Revocation preserves balances and allowances but blocks movement.
48	
49	D5 recovery is an explicit exception: default admin can force-transfer from a nonzero revoked holder to an eligible recipient even while paused. It cannot mint or burn. D6 prevents removing the issuer's default admin role, while compliance authority remains delegable and revocable. An issuer can therefore restore compliance authority, but loss of the issuer's private key remains an operational risk. Delegated administrators share the issuer's powerful trust boundary.
50	
51	AssetFactory rejects zero admin/issuer, self-authorisation of the admin, unauthorised creation and nonpositive supply/price; the enum decoder rejects unsupported asset types. Asset IDs are sequential. Metadata and token/sale addresses are recorded atomically. Empty strings are permitted on chain; the frontend requires a name and symbol. Issuer revocation blocks future creation only. It cannot freeze existing assets. Preventing self-authorisation is a policy check, not protection against a second wallet.
52	
53	AssetSale requires positive quantity, an open sale, eligible buyer, sufficient inventory and exactly quantity × price in wei. Solidity checked arithmetic rejects overflow. Proceeds are recorded before token delivery; a failed transfer reverts token/ETH/accounting changes together. Allocation requires issuer allowance and both issuer/sale eligibility. The factory uses known AssetToken code; separately deployed sales pointing at arbitrary ERC-20 implementations are unsupported.
54	
55	Withdrawal uses checks-effects-interactions: owed proceeds are zeroed before the ETH callback, and rejected payouts revert the accounting. There is no ReentrancyGuard. Sweep pays only forced ETH above owed proceeds. Closure is irreversible and blocks further purchases/deposits. Unsold recovery requires closure and still follows token pause/eligibility rules. Restoring issuer/sale eligibility and unpausing enables ordinary recovery; privileged D5 recovery remains explicit.
56	
57	## Frontend and transactions
58	
59	React routes implement marketplace, asset details/purchase, administration, issuer management and investor portfolio/history. ethers public reads use a configured JsonRpcProvider; wallet writes use BrowserProvider. EIP-1193 events invalidate account/network-dependent roles, balances and forms, and listeners are removed on cleanup. Public registry refreshes retain data to preserve the approval/deposit form; account state is never retained across sessions.
60	
61	All quantities, prices and payments use BigInt with uint256 bounds; ETH input supports at most 18 decimal places. UI address validation rejects zero/invalid addresses. Compiled artifacts supply ABIs. Displayed portfolio balances come from balanceOf, while history comes from contract-scoped event logs. Purchase and forced-transfer companion Transfer events are deduplicated. Metadata is rendered as text, not injected HTML.
62	
63	Transaction state distinguishes wallet approval, submitted hash, pending receipt, confirmed receipt, revert, rejection and unknown confirmation. A receipt timeout retains the hash and disables repeated submission in the active session. Rechecking a real receipt determines success or failure. This state is not durable across page reloads. A malicious provider or a state change after preflight cannot be eliminated by UI checks.
64	
65	Phase 6 fixed AUD-016/SEC-013: signer acquisition now validates factory runtime and deployment block fingerprints through the wallet RPC as well as the public RPC, then rechecks chain/account. Equal chain IDs alone do not identify the same local deployment. The sidebar now names the configured network instead of hardcoding a previous phase.
66	
67	## Validation and security results
68	
69	Fresh baseline: 142 contract/script tests, 118 frontend tests and one local service-integration test passed. Final: 153 contract/script tests, including 11 new adversarial tests; 122 frontend tests, including four signing-deployment regressions; one expanded real-chain service lifecycle. Typechecks and frontend build pass. Two errors in newly generated audit helpers were corrected and their initial failure logs retained.
70	
71	Security tests cover access escalation, direct/delegated compliance, payment boundaries/overflow, insufficient ETH, rollback, two-issuer isolation, revocation recovery, pause and forced transfer. Three deterministic seeds each perform 48 modeled operations. Contract issuer callbacks test repeated withdrawals, cross-function sweeps and rejected payouts. These finite checks are not a mathematical proof.
72	
73	Native coverage reports 100% production contract lines/statements; including test helpers, 99.25% lines and 99.37% statements. Slither scanned 22 contracts with 102 detectors and produced 29 findings, all individually triaged. No new exploitable production-contract issue was confirmed. Root npm audit reports 16 affected development dependency nodes; frontend and root production-only audits report zero. Compiler 0.8.24 has newer advisories whose applicability is discussed, not silently dismissed. See [test results](audit/test-results.md), [findings](audit/security-findings.md), [static analysis](audit/slither-summary.md), [dependency review](audit/dependency-review.md) and [coverage/gas](audit/coverage-summary.md).
74	
75	The exact Phase 6 demonstration executes 31 checks and 18 mined transactions, including three expected reverts. Final CPT balances: issuer 9850, A 80, B 70, sale 0; total supply 10000. The issuer receives 0.15 ETH proceeds, and a separate 5000-unit DLT asset remains isolated. [Receipt/state evidence](audit/final-demo.json) includes addresses, hashes, logs, fees and reverted transactions. This is local evidence, not public-explorer evidence.
76	
77	## Deployment and reproducibility
78	
79	Solidity 0.8.24 with optimizer runs=200 targets Shanghai in both default and production profiles. Hardhat 3.21.0, OpenZeppelin 5.6.1 and ethers 6.17.0 are resolved by lockfiles. Runtime sizes: factory 13545, token 4124, sale 3132 bytes. No production Solidity or dependency version changed in Phase 6; no new gas savings are claimed.
80	
81	Local deployments use chain 31337. Deploy scripts write the factory address, chain, deployment block/hash, runtime hash and ABIs; local records change after each reset. The Sepolia configuration uses chain 11155111 and named config variables/keystore entries, but no verified Sepolia deployment record is present. See the [deployment guide](Deployment_Guide.md).
82	
83	## Remaining limitations and future work
84	
85	A real MetaMask/browser rehearsal and required Sepolia evidence remain outstanding. Browser connection discovery returned no available browser, so no screenshots or browser acceptance are claimed. The assignment PDF was absent; the team must check course packaging and complete identity/contribution fields in the AI report.
86	
87	Production use would require independent review, resolution of compiler/dependency concerns, key governance/recovery design, verified legal/custody arrangements and stronger operational monitoring. Registry/history pagination, durable pending-transaction tracking and explicit UI pause status are possible future refinements. They are not implemented features. The present system is an academic local demonstration, not a production investment platform.
88

98	
99	Missing factory, mismatched code or old block hash means stale configuration or mismatched RPCs: redeploy on the intended chain, sync artifacts and restart the frontend. Pause blocks normal movements, including recovery; unpause/reapprove through the authorised issuer where appropriate.

# Applies one mutant to blockchain.ts in the verification worktree, runs the full frontend suite, restores the file.
param([string]$Worktree, [string]$OutDir)
$file = Join-Path $Worktree "frontend/src/services/blockchain.ts"
$mutants = [ordered]@{
  "M1-drop-ready-provider" = @(@("    await this.ready(provider);`n", ""))
  "M2-ready-ignores-param" = @(
    @("const chain = await provider.getNetwork();", "const chain = await this.provider.getNetwork();"),
    @("const code = await provider.getCode(", "const code = await this.provider.getCode("),
    @("const block = await provider.getBlock(", "const block = await this.provider.getBlock("))
  "M3-blockhash-from-public-rpc" = @(@("const block = await provider.getBlock(", "const block = await this.provider.getBlock("))
  "M4-drop-post-ready-recheck" = @(@("    const [currentChain, currentAccounts] = await Promise.all([", "    /*const [currentChain, currentAccounts] = await Promise.all(["),
                                   @("      throw new Error(`"Wallet account changed. Review the form and try again.`");`n    return provider.getSigner", "      throw new Error(`"Wallet account changed. Review the form and try again.`");*/`n    return provider.getSigner"))
}
$orig = [System.IO.File]::ReadAllText($file)
$nl = if ($orig.Contains("`r`n")) { "`r`n" } else { "`n" }
foreach ($name in $mutants.Keys) {
  $text = $orig
  foreach ($pair in $mutants[$name]) {
    $from = $pair[0].Replace("`n", $nl); $to = $pair[1].Replace("`n", $nl)
    $idx = $text.IndexOf($from)
    if ($idx -lt 0) { throw "$name : pattern not found: $from" }
    if ($text.IndexOf($from, $idx + 1) -ge 0 -and $name -ne "M4-drop-post-ready-recheck") { throw "$name : pattern not unique" }
    $text = $text.Substring(0, $idx) + $to + $text.Substring($idx + $from.Length)
  }
  [System.IO.File]::WriteAllText($file, $text)
  Push-Location $Worktree
  npm test --prefix frontend *> (Join-Path $OutDir "out-$name.log")
  $code = $LASTEXITCODE
  Pop-Location
  $summary = (Select-String -Path (Join-Path $OutDir "out-$name.log") -Pattern '^\s+Tests ').Line
  $failed = (Select-String -Path (Join-Path $OutDir "out-$name.log") -Pattern '^\s+×' | ForEach-Object { $_.Line.Trim() }) -join " | "
  "$name exit=$code $summary"
  if ($failed) { "   failed: $failed" }
  [System.IO.File]::WriteAllText($file, $orig)
}

1	# Final audit and submission readiness — 6 November 2026
2	
3	**Local Phase 6 audit/remediation/documentation work is complete. Full submission acceptance is not yet complete.** The remaining gates are a real MetaMask/browser rehearsal, required Phase 5 Sepolia deployment/receipt evidence, and team review of the original assignment brief and report identity/contribution fields. No assignment PDF was present in this repository.
4	
5	## Results
6	
7	- Fresh baseline: 142 contract/script tests and 118 frontend tests passed; build/typechecks, existing demos and local integration passed after resolving compiler-cache permissions.
8	- Confirmed new issue: SEC-013 / AUD-016, medium, signing RPC deployment not validated. Four failing-before cases now pass. Wallet code/block checks and account/network rechecks implemented. No production Solidity changed.
9	- Final: 153 contract/script tests, 122 frontend tests, one real-chain frontend-service integration test; builds and typechecks pass. Eleven new adversarial contract tests include 144 modeled operations over three seeds and two independent issuers.
10	- Exact demonstration: 31 checks, 18 mined local transactions, three expected reverts. CPT issuer 9850 / A 80 / B 70 / sale 0, supply 10000; 0.15 ETH withdrawn; DLT independent. Full receipt and event evidence: `final-demo.json`.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Usage: scripts/evidence.sh [label]
#
# Runs build, tests, gas report, coverage and (if installed) Slither, and saves
# every output under docs/evidence/runs/<utc time>_<commit>[-dirty][_label]/ so
# each result is tied to a commit. Failing steps are recorded, not hidden: a
# "before fix" run is supposed to show a failing test.
#
# Ported from Foundry to Hardhat 3 after audit-1 F-13: the project never used
# forge, so every earlier run recorded exit 127 for each step.

set -uo pipefail

root=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null) || { echo "Run this inside the git repo." >&2; exit 1; }
cd "$root"

label="${1:-}"
sha=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD 2>/dev/null || echo nocommit)
dirty=""
if [ -n "$(git status --porcelain --untracked-files=no 2>/dev/null)" ]; then
  dirty="-dirty"
fi
ts=$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)
out="docs/evidence/runs/${ts}_${sha}${dirty}${label:+_$label}"
mkdir -p "$out"

{
  echo "utc: $ts"
  echo "commit: $(git rev-parse HEAD 2>/dev/null || echo none)"
  echo "uncommitted changes: ${dirty:+yes}${dirty:-no}"
  echo "label: ${label:-none}"
  echo "run by: $(git config user.name 2>/dev/null || echo unknown)"
  echo "node: $(node --version 2>/dev/null)"
  echo "hardhat: $(npx hardhat --version 2>/dev/null | tail -n 1)"
  echo "slither: $(slither --version 2>/dev/null || echo 'not installed')"
} > "$out/meta.txt"

: > "$out/summary.txt"

step() {
  local name=$1; shift
  echo ">> $name: $*"
  { echo "\$ $*"; echo; } > "$out/$name.log"
  "$@" >> "$out/$name.log" 2>&1
  local code=$?
  printf '%-10s exit %-4s %s\n' "$name" "$code" "$*" >> "$out/summary.txt"
}

step build    npx hardhat compile
step test     npx hardhat test --no-compile
# Gas stats and coverage each need their own instrumented build. With
# --no-compile they print an empty table or 0% and still exit 0.
step gas      npx hardhat test --gas-stats
step coverage npx hardhat test --coverage

if command -v slither >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  # Slither prints the build commands it runs on stdout too; those lines start
  # with a quote and are dropped from the checklist.
  echo ">> slither: slither . --json $out/slither.json --checklist"
  slither . --json "$out/slither.json" --checklist 2> "$out/slither.log" \
    | grep -v "^'" > "$out/slither-checklist.md"
  printf '%-10s exit %-4s %s\n' slither "${PIPESTATUS[0]}" "slither . --checklist" >> "$out/summary.txt"
else
  printf '%-10s skipped    (slither not installed)\n' slither >> "$out/summary.txt"
fi

cat >> "$out/summary.txt" <<'EOF'

Notes: gas and coverage re-run the suite, so they exit non-zero whenever any
test fails; on a "before fix" run that is expected. Slither exits non-zero when
it reports findings; it only failed to run if slither.json says "success": false.
EOF

echo
echo "Saved to $out"
cat "$out/summary.txt"
if [ -n "$dirty" ]; then
  echo "WARNING: uncommitted changes. Commit first if you will cite this run in the report."
fi

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Usage: scripts/evidence.sh [label]
#
# Runs build, tests, gas report, coverage and (if installed) Slither, and saves
# every output under docs/evidence/runs/<utc time>_<commit>[-dirty][_label]/ so
# each result is tied to a commit. Failing steps are recorded, not hidden: a
# "before fix" run is supposed to show a failing test.
#
# Ported from Foundry to Hardhat 3 after audit-1 F-13: the project never used
# forge, so every earlier run recorded exit 127 for each step.

set -uo pipefail

root=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null) || { echo "Run this inside the git repo." >&2; exit 1; }
cd "$root"

label="${1:-}"
sha=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD 2>/dev/null || echo nocommit)
dirty=""
if [ -n "$(git status --porcelain --untracked-files=no 2>/dev/null)" ]; then
  dirty="-dirty"
fi
ts=$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)
out="docs/evidence/runs/${ts}_${sha}${dirty}${label:+_$label}"
mkdir -p "$out"

{
  echo "utc: $ts"
  echo "commit: $(git rev-parse HEAD 2>/dev/null || echo none)"
  echo "uncommitted changes: ${dirty:+yes}${dirty:-no}"
  echo "label: ${label:-none}"
  echo "run by: $(git config user.name 2>/dev/null || echo unknown)"
  echo "node: $(node --version 2>/dev/null)"
  echo "hardhat: $(npx hardhat --version 2>/dev/null | tail -n 1)"
  echo "slither: $(slither --version 2>/dev/null || echo 'not installed')"
} > "$out/meta.txt"

: > "$out/summary.txt"

step() {
  local name=$1; shift
  echo ">> $name: $*"
  { echo "\$ $*"; echo; } > "$out/$name.log"
  "$@" >> "$out/$name.log" 2>&1
  local code=$?
  printf '%-10s exit %-4s %s\n' "$name" "$code" "$*" >> "$out/summary.txt"
}

step build    npx hardhat compile
step test     npx hardhat test --no-compile
# Gas stats and coverage each need their own instrumented build. With
# --no-compile they print an empty table or 0% and still exit 0.
step gas      npx hardhat test --gas-stats
step coverage npx hardhat test --coverage

if command -v slither >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  # Slither prints the build commands it runs on stdout too; those lines start
  # with a quote and are dropped from the checklist.
  echo ">> slither: slither . --json $out/slither.json --checklist"
  slither . --json "$out/slither.json" --checklist 2> "$out/slither.log" \
    | grep -v "^'" > "$out/slither-checklist.md"
  printf '%-10s exit %-4s %s\n' slither "${PIPESTATUS[0]}" "slither . --checklist" >> "$out/summary.txt"
else
  printf '%-10s skipped    (slither not installed)\n' slither >> "$out/summary.txt"
fi

cat >> "$out/summary.txt" <<'EOF'

Notes: gas and coverage re-run the suite, so they exit non-zero whenever any
test fails; on a "before fix" run that is expected. Slither exits non-zero when
it reports findings; it only failed to run if slither.json says "success": false.
EOF

echo
echo "Saved to $out"
cat "$out/summary.txt"
if [ -n "$dirty" ]; then
  echo "WARNING: uncommitted changes. Commit first if you will cite this run in the report."
fi

Verification is complete apart from the integration test. I've found no new code defect, so no AUD-017 so far. Here's where things stand before I ask for your decisions.

**Results so far**
- **Tests:** 153 contract tests and 122 frontend tests pass, as claimed. The typecheck and build pass.
- **Scripts:** the replay passes 12 steps with 34 checks. `auditDemo` passes 31 checks with 18 receipts (15 succeeded, 3 expected reverts), CPT balances 9850/80/70/0 and 0.15 ETH withdrawn. My regenerated demo JSON is identical to the committed one apart from the transaction hashes.
- **Sizes and coverage:** contract sizes are 13545/4124/3132 bytes in both build profiles. The production contracts have 100% line and statement coverage. Including the test helpers I measure 99.43% of lines, not the 99.25% the branch claims; this is minor.
- **Slither:** all 29 findings are classified and each maps 1:1 to a result in the JSON. Slither isn't installed here, so I didn't re-run it.
- **AUD-016 is a real behavioural fix.** Against main's `blockchain.ts`, exactly the 4 new tests fail, because the promise resolved where it should have rejected. Three mutations of the fix each make tests fail. **But deleting the chain/account recheck that runs after validation leaves all 122 tests passing.** The reports claim that recheck, and no test covers it.
- **Secret scan:** 0 dev keys, seed phrases, BIP-39 runs, non-noreply emails, keyed RPC URLs or API keys.
  - Privacy: 334 absolute paths containing one macOS username, all in the Slither JSONs and logs.
  - The commit's author email is a non-noreply work address. It's already on origin.
- **Docs:** every link resolves, all quotes are verbatim, the historical numbers match, and there are no false Sepolia or MetaMask claims. All 99 source-manifest hashes match c7cb0d1.
  - Stale text: about 10 places still say "uncommitted" or "no commits".

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Usage: scripts/new-issue.sh "Short title of the issue"
#
# Creates docs/issues/AUD-NNN-<slug>.md from the template, with the next free
# number, and adds a row to docs/issues/INDEX.md.

set -euo pipefail

root=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null) || { echo "Run this inside the git repo." >&2; exit 1; }
cd "$root"

title="${1:-}"
if [ -z "$title" ]; then
  echo 'Usage: scripts/new-issue.sh "Short title"' >&2
  exit 1
fi

dir=docs/issues
last=$(ls "$dir" 2>/dev/null | sed -n 's/^AUD-\([0-9][0-9]*\)-.*\.md$/\1/p' | sort -n | tail -n 1)
next=$(printf '%03d' $(( 10#${last:-0} + 1 )))
id="AUD-$next"
slug=$(printf '%s' "$title" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' | sed -e 's/[^a-z0-9]\{1,\}/-/g' -e 's/^-//' -e 's/-$//' | cut -c1-50)
file="$dir/$id-$slug.md"

sed -e "s/AUD-XXX/$id/g" -e "s/TITLE/$(printf '%s' "$title" | sed 's/[&/\]/\\&/g')/" "$dir/TEMPLATE.md" > "$file"
echo "| [$id]($id-$slug.md) | $title | | | open |" >> "$dir/INDEX.md"

echo "Created $file"

# AUD-030 / SEC-013: Signing wallet deployment is not checked against the public RPC

Status: fixed in the working tree; severity: medium; category: frontend transaction correctness. Found by Codex during Phase 6 source review and failing regression. Baseline: `0b1249e`. No commits requested or made.

## 1. Why AI made the mistake

The Phase 4 service validates the factory bytecode and deployment block through its public JsonRpcProvider, while signer() separately checks only the wallet chain ID and selected account. The code is AI-assisted according to the Phase 4 session summary; that summary does not preserve the author's exact reasoning. Hypothesis: the implementation treated equal chain IDs as sufficient evidence that both providers reference the same deployment.

## 2. Why it is problematic

Two local RPCs can both use chain 31337 and deterministic factory addresses while containing different contracts or blockchain sessions. The user could see eligibility/inventory from one node and sign on another. Depending on the destination, the transaction may revert or send value to an unintended contract/address. No real funds were lost in this audit; the mismatch is reproduced with a controlled EIP-1193 provider. A malicious provider can still lie about all returned data.

## 3. How the issue was fixed

`Blockchain.ready` accepts either read or browser provider and applies the same chain/code/deployment-block checks. `signer` validates the BrowserProvider before obtaining a signer and then rechecks the wallet's chain and first account. No contracts or financial rules changed. The test fixture returns a valid JSON-RPC block when validation requests it.

## 4. Evidence that the fix works

`frontend/src/test/signingDeployment.security.test.ts`: three negative cases (missing code, different code, different deployment block despite equal chain ID) and one matching-deployment success case. Before: `docs/audit/logs/SEC-013-before.log`, 4 failing; the three negative cases resolved instead of rejecting, while the positive case proved the expected code request was absent. After: `SEC-013-after.log`, full frontend suite 122 passing. Final real-chain integration (`final-integration.log`) passes with actual wallet-side deployment reads. Final build passes.

The issue script created this record. The user's explicit no-commit instruction supersedes the repository's two-commit evidence convention. Raw targeted before/after logs, baseline revision and the final source manifest replace that convention here; no separate evidence.sh run is claimed.

# AUD-030 / SEC-013: Signing wallet deployment is not checked against the public RPC

Numbering: commit c7cb0d1 (origin/phase-6) files this issue as AUD-016. It was renumbered AUD-030 on main on 7 November 2026, because AUD-016 and AUD-017 are used on `frontend-redesign` and AUD-018 to AUD-029 are left for the independent review pass. The raw logs under `docs/audit/logs/`, `docs/audit/source-manifest.json` and `docs/ai-logs/phase6-session.md` keep the original number. See `docs/issues/INDEX.md`.

Status: fixed in the working tree; severity: medium; category: frontend transaction correctness. Found by Codex during Phase 6 source review and failing regression. Baseline: `0b1249e`. No commits requested or made.

## 1. Why AI made the mistake

The Phase 4 service validates the factory bytecode and deployment block through its public JsonRpcProvider, while signer() separately checks only the wallet chain ID and selected account. The code is AI-assisted according to the Phase 4 session summary; that summary does not preserve the author's exact reasoning. Hypothesis: the implementation treated equal chain IDs as sufficient evidence that both providers reference the same deployment.

## 2. Why it is problematic

Two local RPCs can both use chain 31337 and deterministic factory addresses while containing different contracts or blockchain sessions. The user could see eligibility/inventory from one node and sign on another. Depending on the destination, the transaction may revert or send value to an unintended contract/address. No real funds were lost in this audit; the mismatch is reproduced with a controlled EIP-1193 provider. A malicious provider can still lie about all returned data.

## 3. How the issue was fixed

`Blockchain.ready` accepts either read or browser provider and applies the same chain/code/deployment-block checks. `signer` validates the BrowserProvider before obtaining a signer and then rechecks the wallet's chain and first account. No contracts or financial rules changed. The test fixture returns a valid JSON-RPC block when validation requests it.

## 4. Evidence that the fix works

`frontend/src/test/signingDeployment.security.test.ts`: three negative cases (missing code, different code, different deployment block despite equal chain ID) and one matching-deployment success case. Before: `docs/audit/logs/SEC-013-before.log`, 4 failing; the three negative cases resolved instead of rejecting, while the positive case proved the expected code request was absent. After: `SEC-013-after.log`, full frontend suite 122 passing. Final real-chain integration (`final-integration.log`) passes with actual wallet-side deployment reads. Final build passes.

The issue script created this record. The user's explicit no-commit instruction supersedes the repository's two-commit evidence convention. Raw targeted before/after logs, baseline revision and the final source manifest replace that convention here; no separate evidence.sh run is claimed.
